18: ```
19: draft → accepted
20:   L__> archived → (move to 06_Archive/knowledge/)
21: ```

24: - **accepted**: Reviewed and finalized
25: - **archived**: Stale or superseded
26: 
27: ## File system layout
28: 
29: ```
30: 02_Knowledge/
31: └── technologies/
32:     ├── tools/           # CLI tools, software utilities
33:     ├── services/        # specific services (forgejo, homepage, etc.)
34:     ├── kubernetes/      # k8s concepts, patterns, manifests
35:     └── hardware/        # physical hardware, specs, diagrams
36: ```

41:

43: ---
44: title: ""
45: status: draft        # draft | accepted | archived
46: author: ""
47: date: YYYY-MM-DD
48: tags: []
49: sources:
50:   - url: ""
51:     title: ""
52: last_audit_date: YYYY-MM-DD
53: related_docs: []
54: ---
55: ```

60: ---
61: title: "Ingress controllers in Kubernetes"
62: status: draft
63: author: "padawont"
64: date: 2026-08-13
65: tags: [kubernetes, networking, ingress]
66: sources:
67:   - url: "https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/"
68:     title: "Kubernetes Ingress docs"
69: last_audit_date: 2026-08-13
70: related_docs:
71:   - "./05_Implementations/node-main/traefik/overview.md"
72: ---
73: ```
74: 
75: See `./Templates/knowledge/note.md` for a copyable template.
76:

78: 
79: ```
80: # Title
81: 
82: Overview — what is this concept? Why does it matter?
83: 
84: ## Details
85: 
86: Deep dive with examples.
87: 
88: ## Sources / Further Reading
89: ```
90:

92: 
93: ```yaml
94: # simplified, vendor-neutral
95: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
96: kind: Ingress
97: metadata: { name: example-ingress }
98: spec:
99:   rules:
100:     - host: example.com
101:       http: { paths: [{ path: /, pathType: Prefix }] }
102: ```
103:

105: 
106: ```yaml
107: # actual running config, may drift from this doc
108: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
109: kind: Ingress
110: metadata: { name: forgejo-ingress, namespace: forgejo }
111: spec:
112:   ingressClassName: traefik
113:   rules:
114:     - host: git.homelab.local
115:       http: { paths: [{ path: /, pathType: Prefix }] }
116: ```

119: 
120: - **Atomic notes**: one concept per file. When a file hits 150 lines (including frontmatter and blank lines), split it.
121: - Both abstract examples and real configs are welcome — label each block as "Example — abstract" or "Example — real config"
122: - Set `last_audit_date` on every edit; re-audit weekly
123: - Use `related_docs` to cross-link to implementations and vice-versa
124:

126: 
127: | Role | May | Must not |
128: |---|---|---|
129: | `worker` | read, gather sources, create and edit the note | edit files outside its brief, add unsourced claims |
130: | `reviewer` | run all five review types, emit the JSON report | edit, propose unverified fixes |
131: | `editor` | revise the note and its JSON with a cited source or rule | change anything without a citation |
132: | `spec-writer` | append a spec section referencing this note | rewrite or delete note content |
133: | `cluster-worker` | not applicable to this folder | run operational plans here |
134: 
135: Review types: `source`, `accuracy`, `scope`, `structure`, `overlap`.
136: Escalation: anything unresolved goes to the hub in the handoff `blocked:` field — never a guess.

# Backups and Backup Restoration

As your Forgejo installation becomes a critical part of your development lifecycle, the data within it needs to be saved in a backup in order to ensure you don’t lose anything.

Forgejo doesn’t provide or recommend any specific backup tool, but does provide information on what needs to be backed up, how to manage a backup cycle, and how to restore Forgejo to working order from a backup.

## Backing Up Forgejo[](#backing-up-forgejo)

Warning

It is strongly recommended to **shut down** Forgejo during a backup.

Forgejo saves data in multiple different systems, even in its simplest configuration: Git repositories and bulk files are saved on disk as regular files, and a SQL database is used to record information about user interactions. It is not trivial to perform a consistent backup of all that data while Forgejo is running. An inconsistent backup may result in data loss when attempting to restore it.

### Database[](#database)

For SQLite, the database file in the config option [`[database].PATH`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#database-database) needs to be backed up with any file backup tool.

For other databases, use database backup tools that are appropriate to your [selected database engine](../../installation/database-preparation/) to create a backup of the Forgejo SQL database. Any tool designed to work with that database engine should work with Forgejo.

- MariaDB: [mariadb-backup](https://mariadb.com/docs/server/server-usage/backup-and-restore/mariadb-backup/full-backup-and-restore-with-mariadb-backup)

- MySQL: [mysql](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/mysqldump.html)

- PostgreSQL [pg\_dump](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/app-pgdump.html)

Note

With a SQLite database and a default configuration, backing up the `data` folder covers the requirements described in the *Database*, *Repositories*, *Storage*, *Queues*, and *Indexer* sections.

### Repositories[](#repositories)

Forgejo’s repositories are stored on disk. By default, they are in the directory `data` in Forgejo’s [`WORK_PATH`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#overall-default), in a subdirectory `forgejo-repositories`. This configuration may be changed with either [`[server].APP_DATA_PATH`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#server-server) or [`[repository].ROOT`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#repository-repository).

Once you’ve identified the correct folder, you may use any file backup tool to backup this folder when Forgejo is offline.

### Storage[](#storage)

Forgejo’s [storage subsystem](../storage/) is used for the storage of larger files. Each supported subsystem can be configured to store data in local files (called `local`), or in an S3-compatible object storage system (called `minio`).

If using `local` storage, then backing up Forgejo must include all the configured [subsystem directories](../../config-cheat-sheet/#storage.storage). By default, all of these paths are under the directory `data` in Forgejo’s [`WORK_PATH`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#overall-default), but this can be overridden with [`[server].APP_DATA_PATH`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#server-server), or individually on each storage subsystem. Check that every expected path in the [storage subsystem](../storage/) list is in your backup, if they’re applicable to your installation. You may use any file backup tool to backup the locations when Forgejo is offline.

If using `minio` storage, then you should make sure that the remote storage system has appropriate backups, or use a backup tool to keep a copy of the stored artifacts.

### Queues[](#queues)

Background work that is queued but has not yet been executed is stored in a configurable queuing system, defined by the config settings under the [`[queue]`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#queue-queue-and-queue) section. If this data is lost, then queued work will never be completed, which will cause system inconsistencies. These inconsistencies would generally recover over time as new background work replaces the lost work.

If the `[queue].TYPE` setting is `level`, which is the default value, then by default the queues are in the directory `data` in Forgejo’s [`WORK_PATH`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#overall-default), in a subdirectory `queues`. This configuration may be changed with either [`[server].APP_DATA_PATH`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#server-server) or [`[queue].DATADIR`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#queue-queue-and-queue). You may use any file backup tool to backup the locations when Forgejo is offline.

If the `[queue].TYPE` setting is `redis`, then ensure the connected redis server implementation is persistent (not in-memory only), and is backed up.

For the `[queue].TYPE` of `channel` or `dummy`, no backups are possible. Queued background work will be lost when Forgejo is shutdown.

### Configuration Settings[](#configuration-settings)

The Forgejo configuration file, `app.ini`, contains a few critical values that must be backed up in order to restore an instance later. It is recommended that the **entire file is backed up**, but pay specific notice to these configuration settings which contain unique, non-reproducible information:

- [`[security].SECRET_KEY`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#security-security), or the file located at `[security].SECRET_KEY_URI`: some values are encrypted in Forgejo’s database using this key. If it is not preserved between a backup and a restore, then Forgejo will not be able to access the encrypted values. This will break credentials stored in Forgejo, such as webhook credentials, Forgejo Actions secrets, repository mirroring credentials, two-factor authentication configurations, and possibly more in the future.

- [`[oauth2].JWT_SECRET`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#oauth2-oauth2), or the file located at `[oauth2].JWT_SECRET_URI`: OAuth credentials generated by Forgejo are encrypted or signed with this key. If it is not preserved between a backup and a restore, then systems integrating with Forgejo will need to reauthenticate.

- If using `[server].START_SSH_SERVER = true`, the file located at [`[server].SSH_SERVER_HOST_KEYS`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#server-server) and its associated `{...}.pub` file should be included in a backup. If they are not preserved between a backup and a restore, then SSH clients attempting to connect to the Forgejo host will receive SSH host key validation errors. If remote automated mirrors or CI systems are accessing Forgejo, such errors can be tricky to resolve as the host key validity may be saved on first connect, and be difficult or impossible to revalidate.

### Indexers[](#indexers)

Indexers provide the ability to search issues, or search repository code. If the data related to them is lost, then it can be rebuilt, but it may be time-consuming or I/O intensive. Backing it up is recommended for large installations.

#### Issue Indexer[](#issue-indexer)

If the [`[indexer].ISSUE_INDEXER_TYPE`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#indexer-indexer) setting is `bleve`, which is the default value, then bleve data by default is in the directory `data` in Forgejo’s [`WORK_PATH`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#overall-default), in a subdirectory `indexers`. This configuration may be changed with either [`[server].APP_DATA_PATH`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#server-server) or [`[indexer].ISSUE_INDEXER_PATH`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#indexer-indexer). # Backups and Backup Restoration

As your Forgejo installation becomes a critical part of your development lifecycle, the data within it needs to be saved in a backup in order to ensure you don’t lose anything.

Forgejo doesn’t provide or recommend any specific backup tool, but does provide information on what needs to be backed up, how to manage a backup cycle, and how to restore Forgejo to working order from a backup.

## Backing Up Forgejo[](#backing-up-forgejo)

Warning

It is strongly recommended to **shut down** Forgejo during a backup.

Forgejo saves data in multiple different systems, even in its simplest configuration: Git repositories and bulk files are saved on disk as regular files, and a SQL database is used to record information about user interactions. It is not trivial to perform a consistent backup of all that data while Forgejo is running. An inconsistent backup may result in data loss when attempting to restore it.

### Database[](#database)

For SQLite, the database file in the config option [`[database].PATH`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#database-database) needs to be backed up with any file backup tool.

For other databases, use database backup tools that are appropriate to your [selected database engine](../../installation/database-preparation/) to create a backup of the Forgejo SQL database. Any tool designed to work with that database engine should work with Forgejo.

- MariaDB: [mariadb-backup](https://mariadb.com/docs/server/server-usage/backup-and-restore/mariadb-backup/full-backup-and-restore-with-mariadb-backup)

- MySQL: [mysql](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/mysqldump.html)

- PostgreSQL [pg\_dump](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/app-pgdump.html)

Note

With a SQLite database and a default configuration, backing up the `data` folder covers the requirements described in the *Database*, *Repositories*, *Storage*, *Queues*, and *Indexer* sections.

### Repositories[](#repositories)

Forgejo’s repositories are stored on disk. By default, they are in the directory `data` in Forgejo’s [`WORK_PATH`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#overall-default), in a subdirectory `forgejo-repositories`. This configuration may be changed with either [`[server].APP_DATA_PATH`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#server-server) or [`[repository].ROOT`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#repository-repository).

Once you’ve identified the correct folder, you may use any file backup tool to backup this folder when Forgejo is offline.

Forgejo’s [storage subsystem](../storage/) is used for the storage of larger files. Each supported subsystem can be configured to store data in local files (called `local`), or in an S3-compatible object storage system (called `minio`).

If using `local` storage, then backing up Forgejo must include all the configured [subsystem directories](../../config-cheat-sheet/#storage.storage). If using `minio` storage, then you should make sure that the remote storage system has appropriate backups, or use a backup tool to keep a copy of the stored artifacts.

Background work that is queued but has not yet been executed is stored in a configurable queuing system, defined by the config settings under the [`[queue]`](../../config-cheat-sheet/#queue-queue-and-queue) section. You may use any file backup tool to backup the locations when Forgejo is offline.

If the `[queue].TYPE` setting is `redis`, then ensure the connected redis server implementation is persistent (not in-memory only), and is backed up.
